after.problem:
The entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
equals $\frac{2}{5}.$ Find the value of $k.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & k & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2|\begin{aligned}k & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|-3|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}4 & k \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(k-2)-3(4-6)+1(4-3k) \\  & =2k-4+6+4-3k \\  & =6-k.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{21}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{12}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{12} & =(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(4-6) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{21}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{12} \\  & =\frac{1}{6-k}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{6-k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{21}^{′}=\frac{2}{5}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{6-k} & =\frac{2}{5} \\ 2\cdot 5 & =2(6-k) \\ 10 & =12-2k \\ 2k & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Since we want the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{31} & =(-1)^{3+1}|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =24-0 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{13}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31}=\frac{1}{24}\cdot 24=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Determine the entry a13′ in the inverse of a matrix A =[840426102] if its determinant is 24.

a
112
b
−1
c
−124
d
−112
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we want the entry a13′ in A−1, we need to know the value of c31 in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

c31=(−1)3+1|4026|=|4026|=24−0=24.

Then, since A−1=1det(A)CT, we have

a13′=1det(A)c31=124⋅24=1.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating an Element of the Inverse of a 3x3 Matrix
content.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A$ $=[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 6 \\ 1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ if its determinant is $24.$
content.worked_solution:
Since we want the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{31} & =(-1)^{3+1}|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =24-0 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{13}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31}=\frac{1}{24}\cdot 24=1.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
given that $det(A)=4.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
Find the inverse of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
given that $det(A)=4.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
